aiExplanation: This code tries to find the **first "stable" index** — the first position `i` where the largest value seen so far (from the start up to `i`) minus the smallest value from `i` to the end is at most `k`. It builds two helper arrays in a single loop: `maxPrefixSum`, a running **maximum from the left**, and `minSuffixSum`, meant to be a running **minimum from the right** (filled at the mirrored index `j = n - 1 - i`). However, there's a subtle bug: when filling the suffix array it reads `minSuffixSum[j - 1]` (the *left* neighbor, which hasn't been computed yet) instead of `minSuffixSum[j + 1]` (the *right* neighbor), so the suffix minimums are built from uninitialized values and come out wrong — which is why this attempt failed. The final loop then scans for the first index where `maxPrefixSum[i] - minSuffixSum[i] <= k`, returning `-1` if none exists.

author: Vitor
notes: Mistake corrected, performance not really great.
aiExplanation: This code finds the **first "stable" index** in an array — the first position `i` where the gap between the biggest value up to `i` and the smallest value from `i` onward is no more than `k`. In a single clever loop it fills two helper arrays from opposite ends: `maxPrefixSum[i]` holds the **running maximum** of the first `i + 1` elements (built left to right), while `minSuffixSum[j]` holds the **running minimum** from position `j` to the end (built right to left using the mirrored index `j = n - 1 - i` and correctly reading the already-computed right neighbor `minSuffixSum[j + 1]`). A second loop then scans from the start and returns the first index where `maxPrefixSum[i] - minSuffixSum[i] <= k`, or `-1` if no such index exists. This runs in **O(n) time** with two extra arrays of size `n`.

author: Vitor
notes: Improved performance by simplifying to only 1 suffix array.
aiExplanation: This code finds the **first "stable" index** — the first position `i` where the largest value from the start up to `i` minus the smallest value from `i` to the end is at most `k`. It first does a **backwards pass** to build `minSuffixSum`, where each entry `minSuffixSum[i]` is the smallest value in the array from index `i` onward, computed by taking the minimum of the current element and the already-known minimum to its right. Then, instead of storing all the prefix maximums in a second array, it makes a **forward pass** keeping just a single running `max` variable (starting at `-Infinity`), updating it with each element and returning the first index where `max - minSuffixSum[i] <= k`; if the loop finishes without a match it returns `-1`. This is a leaner version of the two-array approach: still **O(n) time**, but with only one extra array instead of two.
